This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blank spaces properly filled in every case. If the name of the child for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or dead, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. Applicable laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard. Fort Lewis Idaho Feb. 23, 1920 Dear Brother Jimmy, I have received your letter and was very glad to hear that you were well and well. Well, you hear that old man Silas died and Lynn Couner Sam Henry flew going after them, and Jim your sister is sick too and want you to come home at once see the supt. about it well it won't be but absent from school for a week and will pay the way expenses to Tacoma again on your return. She's been pretty sick and she is getting worse now and that's why we want you to come home. I can't go no place. I can't leave her. She got to take care of her, and you've got a suit here and some clothes and you might take it back along with you. Well, Jim, I don't know no news about nothing as I never go any place at all nowadays. I can't well. Well, how's the weather down there as it sounds? Tacoma I suppose it's raining and it will. I heard that there was flu at Chemawa School pretty bad. Well, I haven't got much to say now but be sure and come as soon as you can. I am your Brother, Hugh P. Bronchau, As soon as you receive it before you leave. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., March 2, 1920 James Ellenwood Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington Dear James: I am just in receipt of a telegram from the Fort Lupwai Agency advising that it is not advisable for you to come home now. I presume that they have investigated matters and have found that your sister is getting along nicely and it is therefore not urgent that you return home. There is only three months more of school remaining, after which I see no reason why you can not go home for the summer. Very friend, Special Agent in Charge. DHH DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Fort Lapwai Indian School, Lapwai, Idaho, August 28, 1919 E. A. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. My dear Mr. Hammond: Referring to your letter of August 20 inclosing a letter from James Ellenwood, I wish to say that he was at the office some time ago and informed me that he wanted to make a number of purchases before he returned to your school. I told James that whenever he was ready to go to Cushman I would send some money for him and he could make such purchases in Tacoma instead of here. When he arrived here at the close of school I informed him that it would be necessary for him to make his own living during the summer and that I would not give him any allowance during the vacation. Labor was so scarce that boys like James earned from three dollars to three fifty per day, and I felt that giving him his allowance would contribute to the delinquency of this boy. There are some boys who wish to return with him, but as stated in previous letter practically all the Nez Perce children will come under the new regulations promulgated by the Office. However, if any wish to go and pay their way, if they have funds I will be glad to approve the transfer of such. James Ellenwood does not have sufficient funds with which to pay his expenses thru the year, in fact he has very little money to his credit and could not pay any part of his expenses. He has neither parents nor relatives who are willing to assist him. I am returning herewith James' letter. Very truly yours, [signed] Jacob Reid superintendent Wanawai, Wash. Aug 19, 19 Mr. Hammond Lapwai Indian Cushman Trade School Lapwai, Idaho. Will write a few lines and let you know that I am in Wanawai Wash picking prunes now day and I was up at agency and I told Mr. Bried that I want some money to pay my fair all a way to Tacoma Sept 5th and I like to have some money from you this time I told Bried I had some money to go back home and he told if I have some money or not and I told I got some over there and I wish you sent so I could go home more for Sept 5th and I gave some boys to caps over to Cushman school, think they are good boys this time will tell Mr. Hammond. Good By Yours truly, James Allenwood Wanawai Wash. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 10, 1919 James Ellenwood Wawawai, Wash. Dear Jim: I have been waiting for you to arrive at Cushman with the good boys you wrote me about. I have notified Dr. Breid that transportation for you will be made immediately available. If you wish to make the best of your year's work you should report at once. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. May 26, 1919 My dear friend, I will write a few lines and let you know that I am well and find my day. How are you getting along any way we have any fall games over thing this year. Will we have play about before we lost! Now this! some time we get this year. Well I was so glad to hear from you Rose, and I will be glad to hear from you again. Please tell Cloth worker to write to me and I will answer right away, yet, yes. I'm coming home this year again and I am coming back again. Well, we having fine Monday. I have been over Seattle Wash. and having a good old time why don't you come over and try it next year. We all come over at once and have a good old ride on train as we come above. See you will missed a fun one Dunc. She every night now say you know they they don't that because it is about school out the they they use Dunc every night. Well I must close and say good By till we come soon you Be sure and tell her to write to me Rose Well one thing I want to ask you is, are they any Boys got there from here Ashmore Bay they wont call to Tyneham school good By again James Ellwood Ashmore Medicine Trade school Tacona book THE CUSHMAN INDIAN SCHOOL Tacoma, Washington. August 20th, 1919. Dear James:- Your letter of August 19th has just been received. I have on deposit sufficient to pay your return fare to Cushman and will send you transportation September 5th, if you will kindly write me the name of your nearest railroad station. I am very glad indeed that you are planning to come back so early. Doctor Breid seemed to think that some of the returned students were "knocking" the school among their friends, or to him, I don't know which. I am glad to find in your case that you are working in the interests of the school with the evident intention of bringing back with you a goodly delegation of GOOD boys. That's the proper spirit to show. It's a knock at yourself when you knock the school--It isn't the school, it's you. If you are all right, you help make the school all right. The annual catalogue and calendar will be printed this year. It contains a good cut of the baseball teams. As soon as I receive it from the printer, I will mail you a copy and will send copies to the GOOD boys you intend to bring with you September 5th, if you will give me their names and addresses. Where are Leo and Sidney? Mr. James Ellenwood. Sincerely yours, Superintendent. Wawawai, Washington. THE CUSHMAN INDIAN SCHOOL Tacoma, Washington. August 20th, 1919. Doctor Jacob Breid. Superintendent, Ft. Lapwai Indian School. Lapwai, Idaho. My dear Doctor:- I am forwarding herewith a characteristic letter from James Ellenwood asking for money with which to return to Cushman September 5th, 1919. He writes from Wawawai, Wash. James has on deposit here $16.29. Return transportation will be placed to his call either with you, or at Wawawai as you may recommend. James writes that he has some boys to take over to Cushman. In acknowledging his letter, I told him in a postscript to have the boys apply to you for approval of the transfer to Cushman. I will mail him a few forms with specific instructions, and hope that he will bring some of the GOOD boys he mentions with him. As James has funds, he will under the new regulations be required to pay whole or part of his expenses, as you may recommend. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. My dear Mr. Hammond: I regret to report that James Ellenwood did not return to school, as I thought he had, early in September. He called at the office yesterday afternoon and informed me that he had been in Pendleton and Walla Walla, where it was necessary for him to be on account of the round-ups. He promised me that he would call at the office on Monday next, and would arrange to return to Cushman, not later than October 8. I will provide him transportation for returning, and sincerely hope that he will go back without any trouble. Very respectfully, [signature] Superintendent. JB/3 Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington May 21, 1919. Dr. Jacob Breid Supt. Ft. Lapwai School Lapwai, Idaho. My dear Doctor, James Ellenwood has requested me to write you for money. He is asking for $50.00, which I believe to be rather too large an amount. I presume that he wants to get some clothing, and pay his expenses in returning home and leave a sufficient amount here to pay his return transportation at the close of the summer vacation. I am of the opinion that $50.00 is ample for his needs and will recommend the transfer of that amount, provided you have sufficient funds to his credit. Very respectfully, Superintendent. Very respectfully, Supt. 5/21/18 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Fort Lapwai Indian School, Lapwai, Idaho. May 10, 1918 Mr. Jimmie Ellenwood, c/o Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. My Friend: I have just received your letter of May 3rd enclosing your monthly school report, and wish to assure you that I was indeed glad to receive it. I am glad to know that you are contented and getting along well. You have an opportunity to secure an education which you should make the most possible out of, and you should be happy and contented in your work and strive to do the very best you possibly can. It is unfortunate that the Nez Perce boys have gotten rather a bad reputation at the school because of their desertions and I sincerely hope that those remaining in the institution will try to leave a better name than those who have gone. No boy or girl ever gained or accomplished anything by deserting. While I know that you will not do such, I just wish to call your attention to the fact that you have an excellent opportunity and should make good use of it. If you have used your money and the superintendent will so notify me, I will be glad to transfer some more funds to your credit. With best wishes for your success, I remain, Your friend, Jacob Breid Superintendent. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE FORT LAPWAI INDIAN SCHOOL LAPWAI, IDAHO March 17, 1919. Mr. B. H. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. My dear Mr. Hammond: Two Nez Perce boys, who enrolled in your school last year, have decided to return and are leaving this morning for Tacoma, at their own expense. They are James Ellenwood and Sidney Rankin. Please let me know if they report and settle down all right to school work. If they do this, I wish to transfer some of their funds to your supervision. Very respectfully, W. N. Dickel Clerk in Charge. WNS*S Boys arrived March 18th p.m. I shall be pleased to advise you from time to time as to their conduct & progress. Our friend, Cyrus Wilkinson, has begun to show the usual signs of Spring fever & it would not surprise me to hear of his taking French leave at any time. I hope to convince Cyrus however, that it doesn't pay to act the fool—because if he deserts this year, I shall have to express him from school as an habitual deserter— With sincere wishes for Dr. Brint's recovery, and with thanks for your unanimous attention in regarding the value of these two boys. Sincerely yours, [signature] Wushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington March 21, 1919. Mr. W. N. Sickels, Clerk in Charge Ft. Lapwai Indian School, Lapwai, Idaho. Dear Mr. Sickels: James Ellenwood and Sidney Ranken arrived the evening of March 18th. I shall be pleased to advise you from time to time as to their conduct and progress. I hope to convince Cyrus, however, that it doesn't pay to act the fool because if he deserts this year, I shall have to expell him from school as an habitual deserter. With sincere wishes for Dr. Breid's recovery, and with thanks for your personal attention regarding the return of these two boys, I am, Sincerely yours, Superintendent BHH:T Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington March 20, 1919. Feb. 12, 1918 Mr. James Ellenwood, Cushman Trades School, Tacoma, Wash. (Thru the Superintendent) My Friend: I was glad indeed to receive your letter of February 8th and am sorry that you are not well. I feel sure that if you are not well and should return, the superintendent will notify me and make arrangements for your return if he deems such advisable. I do not think it best for you to return home for a visit at this time, for it has been but a short time since you went to Cushman. It seems to me that it would not be wise for you to come home to spend a month with Homer Allen, since you have been back in the school little more than a month. I wish to urge you to do everything you can to fit yourself for your life after you leave the school. Your school days will seem to have been all too short after leaving the institution and you should make the most possible out of the time while you are there. Trusting that you have gotten strong and well, I remain, Your friend, Superintendent. JB R DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Fort Lapwai Indian School, Lapwai Idaho. Feb. 4, 1918 Mr. James Ellenwood, C/o Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. My Friend: I have just heard that you are wanting to return home for the purpose of visiting Hugh Bronche, who is reported to be ill. I am told that he is not seriously ill and I do not believe that it is necessary for you to expend the amount required to make the journey at this time. You know that Hugh has no permanent home and no doubt he is well cared for where he is. It seems to me that the important thing for you to do is to stay with your school work and make good in every way possible. You will not have another opportunity to attend school at Government expense and I wish to urge that you make the most possible out of the time that you are in school. If for any reason we think it best for you to return we will then communicate with the superintendent and make arrangements for your home coming. You have an excellent opportunity to fit yourself for your life work and I again urge that you make the best use of your time. Trusting you are getting along well, I remain, Your friend, Superintendent. DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Fort Lapwai Indian School, Lapwai Idaho. Feb. 4, 1918 Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt. Cushman Trades School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir: Referring to your letter of Jan. 31st with reference to the return of James Ellenwood on account of the request of Hugh K. Bronche, I wish to advise that Hugh has no permanent home, he going from place to place and living with who ever will permit him to do so, and in view of this it would be extremely bad policy to permit James to come to him. This may be only a ruse and I will not give my consent to the return of James at this time. I trust that the boy will get along well and that he will stay with the work until he is thru. Very respectfully, [signature] Jacob Reid Superintendent. JB R Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington, Jan. 31, 1918. Dr. Jacob Breid, Supt. Ft. Lapwai School, Lapwai, Idaho. Dear Doctor: James Ellenwood's check came to hand and has been placed to his credit on our books. James has just received a letter from his brother Hugh K. Broncheau, Gifford, Idaho, telling of his illness, and begging James to return home immediately as he (Hugh) wants to see him so much. I have, for the time being, talked James out of the idea of going home; but as Spring approaches, he will undoubtedly feel the surging of the sap. I will, therefore, appreciate very much a letter from you to James advising him to stick to his school until he has given himself a fair chance to learn a useful vocation. Very respectfully, Superintendent DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Fort Lapwai Indian School, Lapwai Idaho. Jan. 25, 1918. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt. DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Fort Lapwai Indian School, Lapwai Idaho. Jan. 14, 1918 Mr. James Ellenwood, Cushman Trades School, Tacoma, Wash. My Friend: I have just received your letter of Jan. 9th and am glad indeed to know that you are making a special effort to make good. You should do that because it is your excellent opportunity to educate yourself at no expense whatsoever, and you should appreciate this fact and make a special effort to get everything you possibly can out of the short time you will be in school. After you leave, you will realize that the time spent in school was but a short time and you should have made better use of it. I know that your action when deserting was taken without thinking the matter over, and I am also sure such will not occur again. The Government Indian schools will be run in the future for the boys and girls who want the advantages they can get in them, and those who will not willingly and kindly accept such will not be given an opportunity to attend. In view of this, it seems to me that it is of the utmost importance that you make the best possible use of your time while in school. When you want money I would suggest that you call at the office of the Superintendent and have him write for it. That is the best way out of it. I will be glad to see that you have money but prefer that you make your requests thru the Superintendent, since it must be sent to him.
